## Where the Framing Breaks Down

Treating the X-17 through partial simulation misleads in four places.

**It implies the programme reasoned this way.** The similarity analysis above is modern in its framing. The designers knew they could not match velocity and chose to match heat flux, but the binary scaling parameter and the formal statement of three conditions against two knobs are a later way of saying it.

**It assumes a reference re-entry that is generic, and the assumption turns out to carry more weight than it looks.** The 7,000 metres per second at 35 kilometres used throughout is representative, and the actual Atlas condition is not used here. Deriving the reference from the trajectory solution instead shows that it corresponds to a ballistic coefficient of 1,453 kilogrammes per square metre, and that **the heating-rate match fails entirely above about 2,500**. Every ratio in this article inherits that choice, and a reader who prefers a denser reference body gets a materially different answer, up to and including the conclusion that the X-17 could not have matched it at all.

**It treats the trajectory as known.** Murphy and Rubesin plot trajectory parameters for R-2 and R-9, and the flight table gives each successful flight's peak Mach number and altitude, but no full trajectory is tabulated in the public record. The 13.97 kilometre matching altitude is where the vehicle would have had to be to match the reference heating, not a measured altitude, and the article should not be read as asserting the vehicle flew there.

**It gives the vehicle more credit for the shape result than it may deserve.** Blunt-body theory was already published and already believed, and every nose in the X-17 flight table was blunt. The X-17 confirmed rather than discovered, and a confirmation that agrees with the theory it tests is weaker evidence than a surprise would have been.

## The Source Base

**The survey rests on 6,428 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center, together with 72 reports of the Department of Energy's Office of Scientific and Technical Information**, of which 1,382 are report primaries, being 21.5 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. Their median year is 2006. Of the 6,265 dated records, 122, being 2.0 percent, predate 1960, the literature the X-17's own engineers could have read, and 1,571, being 25.1 percent, date from 2019 or later.

**One technical report on the X-17's own flight data is public.** It is [Murphy and Rubesin 1965][research_murphy_rubesin_1965], a contractor report for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA, that analyses the heat-transfer data of flights R-2 and R-9. For the vehicle name, NASA's technical reports server otherwise returns only astronomy false positives, such as the X-ray source GX 17+2. The Lockheed reports that Murphy and Rubesin cite are the R-2 final flight report on transition and heating, LMSD 3003, the R-9 preliminary flight report, MSD 2016 of October 1956, and the summary analysis of the programme, LMSD 2161 of 2 July 1957. Two Lockheed flight reports are catalogued by the Defense Technical Information Center as AD0802033 and AD0802034 but were not retrievable, and no archived copy exists. The flight table comes from the history of the Air Force Missile Test Center for July to December 1957, which is held at Maxwell Air Force Base and is available here only as Heppenheimer reproduces it. The Argus flights are documented in the Defense Nuclear Agency's report.

**The X-17's archival record is thin but not empty.** The [X-16][related_post_a313_bell_x16] was cancelled and left no flight record. The X-17 flew, and two of its flights survive as analysed data, while the rest of its record survives only in summaries.

**The dimensions and launch weight come from secondary compilations, and the flight counts disagree.** The length is 40 feet 4 inches in the reference entry and 40 feet 5.5 inches in Parsch. The research flights number 24 in the Missile Test Center table, 26 in Parsch, and 34 flights in all in the inventory. The research apogees, at 65 to 100 miles, a nominal 400,000 feet and about 500,000 feet, agree to within the spread of the flights, and the 250 miles of the reference entry matches the three-stage ascent used for Argus rather than any research flight.

What does hold the article up is the re-entry literature itself, which is large, public, and contemporaneous. The stagnation heating correlations, the blunt-body theory, the ablation screening programme, the high-temperature air properties, the shock-tube and ballistic-range work, and the free-flight measurement technique are all primary and none is about the X-17.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when it is a NASA Technical Reports Server record, carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports, or is an Office of Scientific and Technical Information report, either at that office's own address or under its 10.2172 prefix. By that rule 939 primaries are Technical Reports Server records, 371 are Defense Technical Information Center reports and 72 are Department of Energy reports.

**The rule undercounts what is first-hand.** Conference papers of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, abbreviated AIAA, and journal papers by the engineers who flew the programmes are primary by any reading and are not reached by an identifier rule. Heppenheimer's history, which reproduces the Missile Test Center flight table, the inventory, the Defense Nuclear Agency's Argus report and the missile directory carry many of the article's facts, and they are cited as curated references outside the survey and are not counted in it at all. **21.5 percent is therefore a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand.**

### Thin Subjects

**Eight subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space and a plural form counted.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| partial simulation and flight duplication | partial simulation, flight duplication, duplication, similitude, similarity law, similarity parameter, similarity requirement | 11 |
| the rocket equation and the mass ratio | rocket equation, mass ratio, Tsiolkovsky, velocity increment, ideal velocity, propellant mass fraction, delta v | 0 |
| binary scaling and the Damköhler number | binary scaling, binary similarity, Damköhler, Damkohler | 5 |
| the total heat load | heat load, total heat, integrated heating, heat input, heat soak | 14 |
| the emissivity of the hot surface | emissivity, emittance, radiative equilibrium, radiation equilibrium, reradiation, radiation cooling, radiative cooling | 15 |
| the effective heat of ablation | heat of ablation, ablation energy, heat of sublimation, heat of pyrolysis | 6 |
| thermal penetration into the shield | penetration depth, thermal penetration, thermal diffusivity, in-depth temperature | 1 |
| the intermittency of transitional heating | intermittency, transitional heating, transitional heat transfer, turbulent spot | 9 |

**The keystone itself is thin in name.** No title in the survey uses the words partial simulation, and eleven name the duplication or the similitude of flight conditions, against 720 records in the facility cluster. **The field practises partial simulation everywhere and names it almost nowhere**, which is why the partition this article draws has to be derived rather than cited.

**The rocket equation and binary scaling are thin for different reasons.** No record treats the rocket equation or a mass ratio, which is a textbook relation the article applies directly. Binary scaling, the similarity the article finds the X-17 overshooting by a factor of 9.25, has five titles, two of them registrations of one paper on shock standoff, so the overshoot is computed here rather than taken from a published comparison.

**Thermal penetration into the shield has a single title.** It is [Altman and Chang 1965][research_altman_chang_1965], a measurement of the thermal diffusivity of refractory materials at high temperature, so the argument that a pulse heats half the depth a soak does stands on the conduction relation the article displays. The effective heat of ablation is named in six, two of them registrations of one paper on meteoroids and one on the inconsistency of the quantity's definition, which is a fair warning about the phenolic-like values the article assumes.

**The total heat load, the emissivity of the hot surface and the intermittency of transitional heating are thin but present**, with 14, 15 and 9 titles. The article's ratio of total heat loads therefore rests on its assumed exposure times, as the text says, and not on a published comparison of a test pulse with a flight soak.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, being re-entry and its partial simulation, the heating, chemistry and radiation of the re-entry environment, the ablators and thermal protection that answer it, the ground facilities and flight experiments that reproduce parts of it, the ballistic missiles and re-entry vehicles the X-17 served, and the successors the review names. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Ablation also names cardiac, hepatic and prostatic surgery, androgen ablation therapy and laser micromachining. Re-entry also names the return of prisoners to their communities, cardiac re-entry and the casing hangers of oil wells. The shock tube is also an instrument of combustion kinetics, atomic spectroscopy, blast simulation and pressure-sensor calibration, and the arc jet is also an electric thruster. The plasma sheath is also a subject of laboratory and fusion plasma physics, stagnation-point flow is also a problem of the mathematics of stretching sheets, and space debris is also a matter of orbital collision risk and space law with no re-entry in it. Ballistic also names armour, gelatine and forensic science, and thermal protection also names diving suits, fabrics and the electronics of hot wells. Correction, erratum and removal notices, book reviews, dictionary headwords and journal front matter are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. Prefaces, forewords and other notices are excluded on the same ground, and so is a second deposit of a document already counted, such as a later server copy of the same report or a conference listing of a paper whose report is kept. News items and the features of trade magazines are excluded as well, whether signed or not, because they report on research rather than argue a result. A signed comment on a paper, a discussion of a paper, the author's closure or reply and a signed letter argue about a result, so each is admitted when the work it answers is on this subject, while an unsigned comment and a referee's report are not.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** The tracking and state estimation of re-entering ballistic targets are kept as the prediction of where a re-entry body goes, but their interception, arms control and missile policy are not. Meteor and meteoroid entry is kept as the natural case of the same physics, and the re-entry of nuclear power sources as the demise problem in its earliest form. The processing and oxidation chemistry of ultra-high-temperature ceramics is materials science rather than flight, and is kept because those materials are what the review says thermal protection became. Solid-motor development is kept for the vehicle's own stages, and air-breathing cruise vehicles for the funding the review describes. Each shares with this subject its physics, its hardware or its customer, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** Records read as off topic have been removed, together with others of their kinds.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact.** Lockheed received a letter contract in January 1955, and quarter-scale vehicles flew from May 1955. The vehicle was a three-stage solid-propellant rocket using a Thiokol XM20 Sergeant first stage and Recruit upper stages, flown over the top with the upper stages firing downward below 100,000 feet. The Missile Test Center table lists 24 research firings from 17 July 1956 to 21 March 1957 with hemispherical, cubic paraboloid, blunt and blunt cone noses, 18 of them successful, peaking between Mach 11.3 and 14.4 at 34,000 to 59,000 feet. The R-2 and R-9 bodies were instrumented copper heat-sink hemispheres of 9 inch diameter, and their data show stagnation and laminar heating in agreement with Fay and Riddell and with Kemp, Rose and Detra, and a boundary layer that became transitional without becoming fully turbulent. The X-17 data contributed to the selection of ablation for Atlas and Titan. A modified X-17a boosted the three Argus nuclear tests of 27 August, 30 August and 6 September 1958 from USS Norton Sound. These facts rest on [Heppenheimer 2007][book_heppenheimer_2007], [Parsch 2003][ref_parsch_x17], [Murphy and Rubesin 1965][research_murphy_rubesin_1965] and [Jones 1982][ref_dna_argus_1982].

**Disputed in the record.** The overall length, given as 40 feet 4 inches and as 40 feet 5.5 inches. The number of flights, given as 24 research firings, as 26 research missiles, and as 34 flights in all. The peak speed, given as Mach 14.4 and as Mach 14.5. Whether the nose cones carried heat-sink protection, which Heppenheimer denies and the contractor report describes for R-2 and R-9. The research apogee spans 65 to 100 miles across the sources, and the 250 miles also published fits the Argus ascent rather than any research flight.

**Engineering analysis, reproducible from the stated inputs.** The requirement that a passive surface reach 4,127 kelvin to reject the matched flux, which exceeds the melting point of tungsten and the sublimation point of graphite and therefore makes ablation mandatory. The Allen-Eggers results, namely a peak deceleration of 43.7 g independent of ballistic coefficient, a velocity at peak heating of 5,925 metres per second also independent of it, and peak-heating altitudes from 31.3 kilometres at a ballistic coefficient of 1,000 down to 12.3 at 13,983. **The ballistic coefficient ceiling above which the X-17 cannot match the heating rate at any altitude, at about 6,300 kilogrammes per square metre even at sea level and about 2,500 at a practical floor.** That the assumed reference corresponds to 1,453. The radiative heating ratios of 110.7 against an intercontinental re-entry and 5,162 against lunar return. The Damköhler ratio of 16.09. The ablation mass loss and recession figures. The thermal penetration depths of 0.93 and 1.89 millimetres. The turbulent heating penalty of 2.70. The free-fall speed of 1,684 metres per second from a 100 mile apogee and the resulting factor of 13.63 in heating rate, with 1,442 metres per second and 21.7 from the nominal 400,000 feet. The factor of 17.58 from the documented stage speeds and the documented upper-stage increment of 2,438 metres per second. The speed range of 3,334 to 4,249 metres per second from the tabulated Mach numbers. The intermittency relation that caps the transitional heating penalty at 2.70. The required density ratio of 27.74 and the matching altitude of 13.97 kilometres. The equal heating rates of 1,398 watts per square centimetre. The stagnation enthalpies of 8.094 and 24.50 megajoules per kilogramme and their ratio of 3.027. The binary scaling ratio of 9.25. The nose radius heating ratios. The ballistic coefficient ratio of 3.33. The Reynolds numbers.

**Inference, and clearly labelled.** That the heating-rate match was fitted to the class of body the vehicle was built to test, and is not a general capability, follows from the ballistic-coefficient ceiling and the coincidence that the assumed reference sits below it. That the X-17 surrendered velocity deliberately, and not as a consequence of what its motors happened to deliver, is likewise inferred. Both are arguments from internal consistency and not from any document. That the chemistry it missed did not matter for the 1956 question is an argument about what could be used rather than about what was true. That the shape result was a confirmation and not a discovery follows from the publication order of the theory.

**Assumed rather than sourced.** The reference re-entry of 7,000 metres per second at 35 kilometres and a 20 degree entry angle. The representative X-17 speed of 4,023 metres per second, taken from the 9,000 miles an hour reported for one flight. The 0.15 metre reference nose radius. The 235 second specific impulse. The mean gravitational acceleration of 9.72 metres per second squared over the fall and the 15 kilometre target altitude. The emissivity of 0.85. The effective heats of ablation, the 1,400 kilogramme per cubic metre density and the thermal diffusivity of the ablator. The 200 kilogramme body and the drag coefficients of 1.0 and 0.3. The body lengths of 1.5 and 0.5 metres. The exposure times of 6 and 25 seconds.

**What the record does not settle and this article does not claim.** What the other X-17 flights measured, since only R-2 and R-9 are analysed in a public report and the Lockheed flight reports were not retrievable. What full trajectory any flight followed. How an ablator would have behaved on an X-17 pulse, since the documented bodies were heat sinks.

**What the contemporary survey changes in the argument.** Two of its observations bear on the article's argument and do not merely extend it. **The chemistry the X-17 surrendered as the cheapest of three requirements is now the most expensive**, because the rest of a modern prediction is comparatively well posed and the model form uncertainty lives in the chemistry. And **the relations are now run in reverse for spacecraft demise**, where ballistic coefficient, ablation rate and heat load are computed to guarantee that a structure comes apart rather than that it survives, and no application demonstrates more sharply how general the physics turned out to be.

**Information postdating the editorial date.** The contemporary literature section is written from current knowledge.

## Out of Scope

The Atlas and Titan programmes themselves are treated only as consumers of this vehicle's result. Operation Argus is named and its physics is not discussed. The Polaris programme is outside this article. The detailed chemistry of dissociating air is cited rather than derived. No attempt is made to reconstruct an actual flight trajectory. Radiative heating is treated only through its velocity scaling, which is sufficient to show that the X-17 could not reproduce it, and the shock-layer radiation transport that would be needed to compute it properly is left to the cited literature.

## Conclusion

The X-17 fired rockets downward because falling was not enough, and the margin is not close. **Free fall from its own apogee would have produced under a tenth of the heating rate it was built to study**, and its peculiar design follows from that factor of fourteen.

What it bought with that architecture was a partial simulation, and the partition is sharp. **It could reproduce the heating rate exactly, in real air, on an instrumented flight body, and it reproduced 33 percent of the stagnation enthalpy and therefore none of the chemistry.** The nonequilibrium state it missed by a factor of nine in the wrong direction, and the total heat load by a factor of four.

**That trade was correct for 1956 and would be wrong today**, and the reversal is the most interesting thing about the vehicle. The programme surrendered the gas physics because it could not yet be computed, and kept the heat flux because every nose cone had to be designed against it. Seventy years later the chemistry is the hard part, the material response is modelled rather than screened, and no facility has yet been built that reproduces the whole condition. **The X-17's compromise has been inherited rather than resolved.**
